subtitle: Every workplace runs on habits that feel normal to the people who set them up. This course shows you how to see whose habits became the rule, who shapes a process and how to make the route usable and fair for everyone.
scope: For staff across DHS and DSD. Use practice cases or nonsensitive process examples, not private personnel or client records. The course does not rate individuals, determine discrimination or authorize changes outside your role. Policy, employment, accommodation, language access and complaint matters stay with their required processes and the person or area responsible. Matters involving Tribal Nations or American Indian communities go to DHS Tribal and Urban Indian Relations and the person or area responsible.
introTranscript: Every team has habits that feel normal: how meetings run, how notices go out, what a form assumes you already know. Those habits came from somewhere, usually from the people who set the process up. They can work well for some people and add extra steps for others, even when no one intends it. This course helps you trace one process step by step. You will ask who shapes the agenda, who receives information and when, and what the rule assumes. You will also connect the process to duties that already exist, such as language access under Title VI and reasonable modifications under the Americans with Disabilities Act. The goal is a route that works for everyone, with clear responsibility and results you can check.

lessons.title: See how expectations and influence shape a process
lessons.summary: Identify a shared expectation and the points where people shape a practice review.
lessons.objective: Identify a shared expectation and the points where people shape a practice review.
objectives: Identify a shared expectation and the points where people shape a practice review.
Distinguish final decision authority from control over the agenda or information.
Explain why better communication alone may not remove a process barrier.
takeaways: Habits and influence can affect the same process.
Control of the agenda and the draft matters, not only the final decision.
Better communication helps, but it is not the whole fix.
lessons.statement: Ask what the expectation is and who can shape each step.

image.caption: Colleagues review a draft and talk through a decision.

intro.heading: See how expectations and influence shape a process
intro.body:
Every team works from shared expectations. One team expects people to raise questions on the spot. Another expects written comments before a meeting. These habits are often useful. They also sit inside a process where some people see the draft early and others see it late. Learning the team’s communication style will not fix a late draft route. Look at both.

Picture a practice proposal review. A coordinator chooses which concerns go on the agenda. An analyst decides who receives the draft. A director makes the final decision. Each role shapes the result in a different way. Do not assume only the final decision maker affects whose information is considered.

Ask what each role is responsible for and how it is carried out. A short draft list may have a real reason, such as privacy. Check that reason rather than assuming bad intent. Also ask whether the familiar route is the only workable one. What information do affected staff need, and when do they need it to respond?

Council of Europe guidance on intercultural education notes that dialogue alone cannot resolve every unequal arrangement. In practice, a good conversation can help you find the problem. It cannot replace a needed change to a rule, a resource or an access route.

inThisLesson: Identify a shared expectation and the points where people shape a practice review.
Distinguish final decision authority from control over the agenda or information.
Explain why better communication alone may not remove a process barrier.
What should Ari look at next?
lessons.keyStatement: Ask what the expectation is and who can shape each step.

flashcards.back: The ability to shape its agenda, information, resources, response or decision. Different roles may hold different parts.
The responsibility a role holds to decide a defined matter.
A step that is simpler for some people because of how the process is set up, not only because of their own effort.
The familiar arrangement treated as the normal starting point. Its effects still need checking.
Input that was received is not proof that it affected the reasoning or the choice.
A recurring feature of a rule, resource or route that limits access, beyond what any one conversation can fix.

items.title: The agenda shapes the question
items.body: A coordinator leaves an access concern off the agenda, so the decision group never discusses it. The coordinator does not decide the matter but still shapes what is seen. Ask how concerns are chosen and where a concern goes if it is left off.

items.title: The draft route shapes who can contribute
items.body: People who see the draft after the choice is made can react, but they cannot shape it. Check the timing and the reason for it. A more respectful meeting does not restore a lost chance to contribute unless the process creates a real way to consider the concern.

items.title: Authority has a defined scope
items.body: Someone must decide the matter, and others supply evidence and experience. You can ask how the decision maker uses input without pretending everyone holds the same approval authority. Keep participation and decision responsibility connected but separate.

tabs.label: Communication only
tabs.body: Clearer, more respectful meetings are a real gain. The same people may still lack the draft or a fair chance to respond. Note the gain, then check which step still limits participation before calling the barrier fixed.

tabs.label: Assuming bad intent
tabs.body: Calling every limited route an abuse skips possible legal, privacy or workload reasons. Check the actual reason and the authority behind it. The useful question is how the arrangement works and what workable alternatives exist.

tabs.label: Tracing the whole route
tabs.body: Trace the expectation, information, agenda, resources and decision responsibility together. This can show a practical improvement and who has authority to make it. Communication learning keeps its place without being asked to settle a process question alone.

check.question: A team discusses respectfully, but affected staff receive the draft only after the choice is made. What still needs a closer look?
check.correct: The information and decision route, including any real limits, and a workable way to consider affected staff’s concerns.
wrong: Whether respectful tone proves everyone had equal influence.
Whether every decision maker should lose authority.
Whether the late recipients understand the team’s culture well enough.
check.feedbackCorrect: The open question is about the arrangement and the chance to contribute. Tone and personal traits do not answer it.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Tone does not show influence. Removing all authority ignores real responsibility. Judging the late recipients moves attention from the route to the people. Check draft timing, any information limits and the route for relevant input before calling the barrier fixed.

items.text: Staff are expected to ask questions out loud during the meeting.
A coordinator chooses which concerns go on the agenda.
Can affected staff respond before the choice is made?
The team treats quick verbal replies as the normal way to contribute.
One role controls who receives the review draft.
What reason requires the short distribution list?

lessons.next: Next: Recognize an easier route without ranking anyone

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Practice lead Ari makes meetings more respectful, but affected staff still receive drafts after decisions are made. Ari wants to report that every participation barrier is now gone.
scenario.prompt: What should Ari look at next?
options: Report that the respectful tone shows everyone now has equal influence.
Review the draft and decision route with the person responsible, keeping real limits and finding a workable way for affected staff to respond in time.
Ask the late recipients to adapt to the team’s meeting style.
responses: The tone changed, but the timing did not. Affected staff still cannot shape a choice that is already made.
This keeps the meeting improvement and addresses the step that still blocks contribution. It also works through the person responsible for the route.
The barrier is the timing of the draft, not the recipients’ style. Asking them to adapt leaves the route unchanged.

lessons.transfer: Using an invented review or a practice case, map the shared expectation, who sets the agenda, who receives the draft and who decides. Name one barrier that better communication alone would not remove.

move.control: You can trace a process and raise a concern through the route responsible for it.
move.failure: A friendlier meeting is used to hide an unchanged access or decision barrier.
move.next: For one process you use, write down who sets the agenda, who sees the draft and when.

lessons.title: Recognize an easier route without ranking anyone
lessons.summary: Distinguish demonstrated effort from an easier route the process provides.
lessons.objective: Distinguish demonstrated effort from an easier route the process provides.
objectives: Distinguish demonstrated effort from an easier route the process provides.
Explain why one easier route does not describe a whole life.
Name a process question about access without rating any person.
takeaways: Effort and an easier route can exist together.
One advantage is not a person’s whole story.
Look at the route and its effects, not at anyone’s worth.
lessons.statement: Name where a benefit comes from without judging the whole person.

image.caption: Two colleagues read the details of a printed notice together.

intro.heading: Recognize an easier route without ranking anyone
intro.body:
Some advantages come from how a process is set up, not only from effort. Knowing an unwritten contact, getting an early draft or fitting the default form can make a process easier to use. That does not mean the person did not work hard. It means effort may not explain every difference in access.

Some trainings call this idea privilege, a term made widely known by Peggy McIntosh’s essay in the late 1980s. In plain words, it means an easier route a person did not have to earn. This course uses the plain description and looks at specific routes rather than labels for people.

Research shows why routes matter. In a field experiment, Bertrand and Mullainathan sent matched résumés to employers in Boston and Chicago. Résumés with names common among white applicants received about 50 percent more callbacks than identical résumés with names common among Black applicants. Equal qualifications on paper did not produce equal first steps.

Now picture a practice unit. A well-connected employee hears about a development opportunity before the wider notice goes out. Their skill may be real. The early notice is still a benefit others did not get. Title VII and the Minnesota Human Rights Act prohibit discrimination in hiring, promotion, training and other terms of employment. A notice that reaches everyone at the same time, with criteria stated in advance, keeps the opportunity open on the same terms.

Keep different kinds of advantage separate. One example about insider information does not show a pattern by race or any other group. A pattern needs relevant data, reviewed through the right process.

Name a process question about access without rating any person.
What is the better question?
lessons.keyStatement: Name where a benefit comes from without judging the whole person.

items.title: Effort and access exist together
items.body: The employee may have built a real skill and also received early information. Naming the early notice does not erase the skill. It asks whether others had a fair chance to show relevant qualifications under the same criteria.

items.title: A life is not a score
items.body: A person may face serious difficulty in one part of life while benefiting from one arrangement. A single overall label would flatten that and could pressure people to share private history. Keep the question on the specific process and benefit.

items.title: A pattern needs its evidence
items.body: One insider-information case points to a route worth checking. It does not establish a pattern across the agency. If a concern involves race or another group, use suitable data and definitions through the right process instead of assuming the conclusion.

tabs.label: Effort only
tabs.body: An effort-only account can miss benefits the arrangement supplied, such as early information. It may read an unequal chance to learn about a task as a difference in motivation. Recognize demonstrated skill and also check whether the opportunity reached everyone.

tabs.label: A label for the whole person
tabs.body: A single label treats one benefit as a full account of someone’s life or worth. It can erase real difficulties and push people to disclose private matters. The useful question names the specific advantage, its source and its effects.

tabs.label: A specific route question
tabs.body: A specific question asks who received the benefit, through which route and with what evidence. It can fix the early notice while keeping real skill and eligibility questions intact. State what the example cannot show, such as a pattern across the agency.

check.question: A skilled employee hears about an opportunity early through an insider route. Which account is most useful?
check.correct: The skill and the early notice exist together; review the notice route and its effects without rating the person.
wrong: Real skill proves the notice route cannot matter.
One benefit proves the person has never faced difficulty.
One process example proves a pattern across all of DHS.
check.feedbackCorrect: This account separates the sources of the advantage and stays within what the evidence shows.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Skill does not erase a difference in access. One benefit cannot describe a whole life. One example cannot establish an agency-wide pattern. Look at the actual route and its effect, using relevant evidence.

items.text: The employee demonstrates the task skill.
The employee hears about the opportunity before others.
One benefit proves an easy life.
A relevant work sample shows proficiency.
The default form fits some staff without extra steps.
One contact example proves a pattern by race.

lessons.next: Next: Examine whose default becomes the rule

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Practice lead Beau says an employee’s strong work proves early insider information gave no advantage. A colleague responds that the employee has had everything handed to them.
options: Accept one of the two views without looking at how the notice traveled.
Ask the employee to list the hardships they have faced.
Recognize the employee’s demonstrated work and review how the notice traveled, whom it reached and when.
responses: Both views skip the route itself, which is the part the team can actually check and fix.
Private history is not needed to review a notice route, and asking for it puts pressure on the employee.
This keeps the employee’s effort in view and puts attention on the route the team can change.

lessons.transfer: Using an invented example or a practice case, describe one demonstrated skill and a separate easier route the process provided. Name one broader claim the example cannot support.

move.control: You can examine a specific route without denying anyone’s effort or judging a whole life.
move.failure: The discussion turns into denying any advantage exists, or into labeling whole people.
move.next: Check whether the next opportunity notice in your area reaches everyone at the same time, with the criteria stated.

lessons.title: Examine whose default becomes the rule
lessons.summary: Identify a familiar default in a practice service instruction.
lessons.objective: Identify a familiar default in a practice service instruction.
objectives: Identify a familiar default in a practice service instruction.
Explain, with a documented Minnesota example, how a written default can shape access for generations.
Compare a workable alternative against civil rights duties and the real requirement.
takeaways: A rule that looks the same for everyone can fit people unevenly.
History shows written defaults can last for generations.
Improve access while keeping the actual requirement.
lessons.statement: Check the ordinary route. Looking neutral is not the same as working for everyone.

image.caption: A presenter walks colleagues through each step of a process chart.

intro.heading: Examine whose default becomes the rule
intro.body:
A default is the route a process assumes. It can look neutral because everyone gets the same words and the same steps. Its effects can still differ when people have different language, information, disability or resources. The question is not whether sameness always fails. It is whether people can actually use the process to meet its real requirements.

Minnesota history shows how long a written default can last. In the first half of the 1900s, many property deeds in Minneapolis and nearby areas included racial covenants. These clauses barred people who were not white from buying or living in a home. Mapping Prejudice at the University of Minnesota has documented tens of thousands of them. Courts stopped enforcing covenants after the 1948 Shelley v. Kraemer decision, and Minnesota barred new ones in 1953.

The effects did not end when the clauses did. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis reports that Minnesota has one of the widest gaps in the nation between white and Black homeownership rates, and connects that gap to this history. A rule written around one group’s expectations shaped who could build wealth through a home.

Today’s defaults are usually quieter. In a practice service instruction, everyone is sent to the same online step, which names a document by shorthand. People who know the process finish quickly. Others must search for a contact or give up. The instruction is consistent, but it relies on knowledge not everyone has.

Civil rights duties already address this. Under Title VI, programs that receive federal funds must take reasonable steps to give people with limited English proficiency meaningful access. Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, public entities must make reasonable modifications to policies and practices when needed to avoid disability discrimination. Check the requirement, test the instruction with people who use it and keep the real eligibility rule unless the responsible process changes it.

Explain, with a documented Minnesota example, how a written default can shape access for generations.
Compare a workable alternative against civil rights duties and the real requirement.
What should Cleo do?
lessons.keyStatement: Check the ordinary route. Looking neutral is not the same as working for everyone.

items.title: The default relies on insider knowledge
items.body: The instruction names a document by shorthand without saying what it is or where to find it. Familiar users move on; others must guess. Review the instruction and a clarification route instead of treating the extra work as a sign that the person is less capable.

items.title: A burden is not proof of a motive
items.body: An unclear or inaccessible route needs attention even when no one intended harm. Describe the feature and the evidence of its effect. Motive and effect are different questions, and you can fix a barrier without guessing at anyone’s intent.

items.title: The alternative keeps the requirement
items.body: A clearer instruction can name the needed document while keeping the actual requirement. The person or area responsible confirms the meaning and the access options. Do not remove eligibility conditions on your own or promise that one rewrite will end every gap.

tabs.label: Identical route
tabs.body: An identical route supports consistency but can still depend on knowledge or access that varies. Ask whether people can understand and use it under its real requirements. Consistency is useful evidence about administration, not proof that every barrier is gone.

tabs.label: Assuming from identity
tabs.body: Assigning someone an alternate route because of a group they belong to is another unsupported prediction. Ask about the actual need, such as a language or an accommodation, and offer the option to everyone it could help.

tabs.label: Usable alternative
tabs.body: A usable alternative addresses a defined barrier and keeps the task’s real requirement. A plain-language instruction or a clear contact can reduce guessing. Confirm it with the person or area responsible, test it with people who use it and check the result.

check.question: An identical instruction depends on knowledge some users do not have. What should staff look at?
check.correct: Whether the instruction and a clarification route can be made usable while keeping the actual requirement and the responsible review.
wrong: Whether identical wording proves equal access.
Which group is less able to understand the process.
Whether the requirement can be dropped without authority.
check.feedbackCorrect: This question addresses the default’s effect without stereotypes or an unauthorized shortcut.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Identical wording does not settle whether people can use it. Group labels replace a process question with a stereotype. Dropping a requirement goes beyond your authority. Check the explanation, the evidence and a workable access route with the person or area responsible.

items.text: The instruction uses unexplained document shorthand.
Identical wording proves equal access.
Can a clearer explanation keep the actual requirement?
The notice is offered only in English.
One group is unable to understand the process.
Which language access or accommodation route applies?

lessons.next: Next: Distinguish being heard from having influence

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Practice process lead Cleo sends one instruction to everyone and believes this proves equal access. The instruction depends on document knowledge that some users do not have.
options: Review the instruction with the person responsible, test a clearer version with people who use it and confirm the actual requirement.
Conclude that users who struggle are less capable.
Drop the document requirement without review.
responses: This fixes the route while keeping the requirement and the responsible review in place.
The conclusion does not explain or repair the missing information.
A usability concern does not give anyone authority to remove a requirement.

lessons.transfer: Using an invented process or a practice case, describe a default, who may need extra steps to use it, what evidence you would check and one workable improvement within your authority.

move.control: You can identify a default’s practical burden and propose a suitable review.
move.failure: A familiar arrangement is treated as neutral only because it looks identical for everyone.
move.next: Read one instruction your area sends out and list what it assumes the reader already knows.

lessons.title: Distinguish being heard from having influence
lessons.summary: Identify input, consideration and influence in a practice decision sequence.
lessons.objective: Identify input, consideration and influence in a practice decision sequence.
objectives: Identify input, consideration and influence in a practice decision sequence.
Explain a decision point that limits meaningful contribution.
Write a response that shows what was considered without promising automatic adoption.
takeaways: A comment count does not measure influence.
Report what was considered and what changed, separately.
lessons.statement: Trace what happened to the concern, not only whether it was collected.

image.caption: Colleagues around a meeting table consider comments on a proposal.

intro.heading: Distinguish being heard from having influence
intro.body:
Collecting views matters, but it does not show that those views affected a decision. A concern may be recorded, considered and not adopted for a stated reason. Or it may change the option or the next question. These are different outcomes. Describe them accurately rather than calling every invitation influence.

In a practice proposal review, affected staff are invited to comment after the choice is fixed. Their views are recorded, but there is no way to revisit the issue. The team can say it received input. It cannot say the input shaped the original decision. Ask what is still open and what response or later review is possible.

When a decision is still open, explain the question, the limits and who decides. Contributors need enough information to know what their input can affect. Meaningful participation does not mean adopting every suggestion or giving every participant decision authority. It does mean relevant concerns get a real chance to be considered.

Close the loop with a clear account: what was raised, what was considered, what changed or did not change, and why. Written reasons help people see that the same standards applied to every comment. If there is no evidence of an effect, say so. A response should never expose private accounts just to prove participation happened.

inThisLesson: Identify input, consideration and influence in a practice decision sequence.
Explain a decision point that limits meaningful contribution.
Write a response that shows what was considered without promising automatic adoption.
What is the better account?
lessons.keyStatement: Trace what happened to the concern, not only whether it was collected.

items.title: Input arrives after the choice
items.body: The team invites comments when the original option is no longer open. Record the timing honestly and ask which response route remains. Do not use the number of invitations as proof that people influenced a choice they had no chance to shape.

items.title: Considered is not the same as adopted
items.body: A concern is reviewed, and the option stays the same because of a stated requirement. That is consideration, even if the person disagrees. It would be inaccurate to say the suggestion changed the option. Describe the review and the reason.

items.title: Influence leaves a trace
items.body: A concern leads the team to add an access question, revise an option or change a next step. Name that effect and its scope. The record can show influence without revealing anyone’s identity or claiming every affected person took part.

tabs.label: Count the comments
tabs.body: A count describes activity but does not show what the decision did with the comments. Timing, substance and response may differ. Use the count for what it is, and check whether relevant concerns had a real chance to be considered.

tabs.label: Promise adoption
tabs.body: Promising to adopt every suggestion makes participation look powerful but can bypass evidence and responsible judgment. Some concerns change an option; others lead to a stated reason or further review. Be clear about the question and who decides.

tabs.label: Trace consideration and effect
tabs.body: State the concern, the response and the actual change, or the reason the option stayed. This links listening to the decision while keeping limits and responsibility clear.

check.question: Comments were collected only after the original choice was fixed. Which statement is accurate?
check.correct: Input was received after the choice; its influence on that choice is not established, and the remaining response route should be made clear.
wrong: The number of comments proves equal influence.
Every suggestion must automatically replace the decision.
The contributors’ backgrounds make their concerns irrelevant.
check.feedbackCorrect: This statement fits the timing and scope of the participation and leaves a clear next question.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Counts do not prove influence. Automatic adoption skips judgment and authority. A person’s background does not make a work concern irrelevant. Explain what was open, what happened to the input and what response or review remains.

items.text: The team records a comment after the choice is made.
A concern leads to a revised access question before the decision.
Every invitation proves equal influence.
The team receives a written concern.
The team explains in writing why a reviewed suggestion was not adopted.
A high comment total proves every affected view was considered.

lessons.next: Next: Choose a process improvement with clear responsibility

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Practice coordinator Drew collects comments after the choice is fixed and wants to report equal influence. One concern may still fit a later review by the person responsible.
options: Use the number of comments as proof of influence on the original choice.
State when input arrived and what it could affect, then name the remaining response or review.
Set the concern aside because it came from people outside the usual group.
responses: The count does not show that anyone had a chance to shape the original choice.
This makes the account honest and gives the concern a practical next step.
Who raised a concern does not decide whether the concern is relevant to the work.

lessons.transfer: Using an invented decision or a practice case, write the sequence of input, consideration, actual effect and one limit. Name what the invitation alone cannot show.

move.control: You can make clear what happened to a work concern, within your role.
move.failure: Collected views become a claim of influence without evidence of any response.
move.next: On the next decision you help with, write down what was raised, what was considered and why the result came out as it did.

lessons.title: Choose a process improvement with clear responsibility
lessons.summary: Distinguish one-to-one help from a process change in a practice case.
lessons.objective: Distinguish one-to-one help from a process change in a practice case.
objectives: Distinguish one-to-one help from a process change in a practice case.
Identify the role and evidence needed for an authorized improvement.
Define a result question about the barrier, not about how people feel about the change.
takeaways: Different barriers need different kinds of action.
Learning and consultant guidance support staff; they do not replace staff responsibility.
A process change needs authority, the same criteria for everyone and follow-through.
lessons.statement: Match the action to the part of the arrangement that creates the barrier.

image.caption: Colleagues around a conference table plan the steps of a process change.

intro.heading: Choose a process improvement with clear responsibility
intro.body:
Some problems improve with a clearer answer or a respectful reply. Others need a change in who gets information, the criteria used, resources or a recurring decision route. A conversation about culture can help find the concern. It cannot authorize a rule change or supply a missing resource.

In a practice development process, opportunity notices travel through personal contacts and reach many staff after selection. Telling staff to network more may help a few people but leaves the arrangement unchanged. A process proposal asks the person responsible to review a notice route that reaches everyone, criteria stated in advance and a fair response time.

Every option must stay open to all staff on the same terms. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s March 2025 technical assistance explains that limiting training, mentoring or other opportunities by race or another protected trait can be unlawful, whatever the goal. The fix is a fair route for everyone, not a route reserved for some.

The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant can offer guidance, knowledge and feedback while staff and decision makers do the work. Make clear who prepares the evidence, who may change the arrangement and who will check its effect. Choose a result question tied to the barrier. Did the notice reach staff in time? Could they find the criteria? Did questions get answers?

inThisLesson: Distinguish one-to-one help from a process change in a practice case.
Identify the role and evidence needed for an authorized improvement.
Define a result question about the barrier, not about how people feel about the change.
What is the stronger response?
lessons.keyStatement: Match the action to the part of the arrangement that creates the barrier.

items.title: One-to-one help has value
items.body: A manager explains the current route and answers a question respectfully. That helps the person use today’s process. Recognize the help and ask whether the recurring late notice still needs a process change; one helpful reply does not fix the distribution rule.

items.title: The process proposal is specific
items.body: The team proposes a notice route that reaches everyone, criteria posted with the notice and a review date. The person or area responsible checks feasibility and limits. Staff prepare the information and options, with consultant guidance when useful.

items.title: The result question follows the barrier
items.body: If the concern is late notice, measure who received it and when, not compliments about the new notice. A defined question helps find what is still unresolved. Avoid rating individual staff or claiming one change has fixed every barrier.

tabs.label: One-to-one help only
tabs.body: Helping one person through a difficult route is useful but leaves the burden unevenly spread. Telling everyone to find an insider contact does not address the late-notice arrangement. Pair the help with a process review when the barrier keeps recurring.

tabs.label: Unauthorized redesign
tabs.body: Changing a rule without authority can bypass legitimate criteria, privacy or decision duties. A good purpose does not grant permission to change every rule. Prepare evidence and a workable proposal, then use the person or area responsible to decide and carry it out.

tabs.label: Responsible process improvement
tabs.body: A responsible improvement defines the barrier, the option, the authority and the result question. It applies the same criteria to everyone and records the reasons for decisions. Staff do the work with guidance, and the result can show a clear gain and what remains.

check.question: What best addresses an opportunity notice that keeps reaching staff late?
check.correct: Prepare evidence and a workable proposal for a notice route that reaches everyone, with criteria stated, and check whether notices arrive in time.
wrong: Tell everyone to rely on personal contacts and treat the problem as solved.
Remove all selection criteria on your own.
Offer an early notice only to staff in selected groups.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response matches a recurring arrangement to a specific, authorized change that applies to everyone, with follow-through.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Personal contacts leave the route unchanged. Removing criteria goes beyond your authority and drops needed safeguards. An early notice for selected groups treats staff differently by group and recreates the same problem. Prepare the proposal and keep the decision with the person responsible.

items.text: Explain the current route respectfully to a staff member.
Propose a notice route that reaches every eligible employee at the same time.
Remove selection criteria without authority.
Answer a question about the existing instructions.
Define what to measure and set a review date for notice access.
Send the notice early to one group of staff only.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Practice team lead Ember sees opportunity notices travel late through personal contacts. Ember proposes more networking advice and wants the consultant to do all the process analysis.
options: Keep networking advice as the whole solution.
Remove every criterion without the person responsible.
Have staff prepare a specific notice proposal with evidence, using consultant guidance, and take it to the person responsible.
responses: Helpful advice does not change the recurring information route.
The concern does not give anyone authority to bypass criteria or formal responsibility.
This builds staff skill and leads to a workable process change through the right decision route.

lessons.transfer: Using an invented process or a practice case, plan one improvement: the barrier, the one-to-one help, the process option, the evidence, who does the work and who decides.

move.control: You can prepare a process review and ask for guidance while keeping responsibility for your own work.
move.failure: A process concern is reduced to better manners, or handed entirely to the consultant.
move.next: Pick one recurring barrier you have seen and write the result question that would show whether a fix worked.

lessons.title: Review results without overstating success
lessons.summary: Interpret a practice process gain alongside a remaining unequal effect.
lessons.objective: Interpret a practice process gain alongside a remaining unequal effect.
objectives: Interpret a practice process gain alongside a remaining unequal effect.
Write a qualified result and a responsible next action.
takeaways: A gain can exist alongside a remaining barrier.
Missing information is unknown, not reassuring.
Keep every claim tied to its evidence and scope.
lessons.statement: A sound review names both the progress and what is still unresolved.

image.caption: A facilitator records results on a whiteboard while the group reviews them.

intro.heading: Review results without overstating success
intro.body:
A clearer process may improve access in one way while leaving another barrier. More staff may get a notice in time, but a required format may still be hard to use. Report the gain and the remaining issue together. One improvement cannot show that every unequal effect is gone.

In a practice review, timely notice improves. The team has no evidence yet about whether the explanation and response route work for people using assistive technology or another language. No recorded complaints does not prove satisfaction or equal access. Name the missing question and a suitable way to check it.

Check who actually received the information. Where data allow, break results down by relevant groups, such as language or disability, to see whether the change reached everyone. The DHS Equity Policy and the Equity Analysis Toolkit both call for measuring results and revisiting a decision. Looking at results by group is a check on the route, not a reason to treat anyone differently.

Write a qualified account rather than a verdict about the people involved. The route reached more people before the deadline; evidence on usability is incomplete; the person responsible will review the next change on a set date. If a complaint or a formal rights issue comes up, use its required process right away rather than waiting for course learning to finish.

inThisLesson: Interpret a practice process gain alongside a remaining unequal effect.
Distinguish missing evidence from reassurance.
Write a qualified result and a responsible next action.
What should the review say?
lessons.keyStatement: A sound review names both the progress and what is still unresolved.

items.title: Report a clear, bounded gain
items.body: More staff receive the notice while they can still respond. That supports a claim about timing. It does not show that every criterion, explanation or response route works. Keep the scope explicit so the gain guides further work.

items.title: No complaint is not a full result
items.body: A person may not know the complaint route, may have no reason to respond or may face another barrier. Silence cannot tell these apart. Record missing evidence as unknown and plan a way to check it.

items.title: The next step stays accountable
items.body: The person or area responsible reviews the notice’s usability and explains the next action. Staff can prepare evidence and seek guidance. Do not delay a formal issue for more learning, and do not turn the result into a rating of staff.

tabs.label: Total success
tabs.body: Declaring total success can hide effects that remain and make later concerns feel unwelcome. One timing improvement does not answer every access question. State the supported gain and what is still unknown.

tabs.label: No progress
tabs.body: Declaring no progress because one issue remains also distorts the result. Timely notice may be a real improvement worth keeping. Name both the gain and the barrier that continues so the next step targets the right problem.

tabs.label: Qualified follow-through
tabs.body: Qualified follow-through links the result to the next responsibility. It separates what improved, what is unknown and what happens next, with a date to revisit. It relies on evidence rather than reassurance.

check.question: Timely notice improves, but evidence about usability is missing. What is the sound result?
check.correct: Report the timing gain, record usability as unknown and name how the person responsible will check it next.
wrong: No complaints prove every barrier is gone.
The gain has no value because one question remains.
The result shows which staff members are most committed.
check.feedbackCorrect: The result keeps both the observed gain and the missing evidence in view.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Silence cannot prove equal access. An open question does not erase the timing gain. Process results are not a measure of individual staff. Report the scope, the unknowns and the responsible next step.

items.text: More staff receive the notice before the deadline.
Whether the explanation works with screen readers has not been checked.
No complaints prove every barrier is gone.
The notice now names a contact for questions.
Whether the notice reached staff who read in another language is not yet known.
Who responded shows which staff care most.

lessons.next: Look at culture together with influence, access and evidence. Pursue improvements through the person or area responsible, apply the same standards to everyone and check the results.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Practice lead Finn sees better timing but has no evidence about usability. Finn wants to declare the whole process fair because no complaints were recorded.
options: Describe the timing gain and the missing usability evidence, then name the next check and a date to revisit.
Declare complete success because no complaints were recorded.
Judge staff commitment by who responded to the notice.
responses: This keeps progress, uncertainty and responsibility visible.
The absence of complaints does not establish a result that was never checked.
Response patterns cannot support judgments about individual staff.

lessons.transfer: Using an invented result or a practice case, write a supported gain, one unknown, the responsible next action, a date to revisit and one claim the evidence cannot support.

move.control: You can report a qualified result and support the next responsible review.
move.failure: Progress reporting hides missing evidence or turns into a judgment of people.
move.next: State what improved, what is still unknown, who handles the next step and when it will be revisited.

jobAid.subtitle: Trace one process: whose default it reflects, who shapes it and who can use it.
remember: Better communication alone cannot remove every process barrier.
Effort and an easier route can exist together.
Look at routes and results, not ratings of people.

sections.heading: Map the arrangement
items: Name the shared expectation and what the process treats as the default.
Identify who sets the agenda, who receives information and when, what resources are needed and who makes the final decision.
Describe a possible easier route or extra burden and the evidence needed to check it.

sections.heading: Check the duties that already apply
items: Language access: under Title VI, take reasonable steps so people with limited English proficiency have meaningful access.
Disability: under the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504, make reasonable modifications and communicate effectively.
Employment: under Title VII and the Minnesota Human Rights Act, keep opportunities open to everyone on the same terms.

sections.heading: Choose the response
items: Separate one-to-one help from a needed process change.
Apply the same stated criteria to everyone, use a second reader where it helps and record written reasons.
Trace input, consideration and actual influence rather than counting comments.

sections.heading: Review and follow through
items: Check who actually received the information, and test notices with people who use them.
State the supported gain and the open question at their proper scope; treat missing evidence as unknown.
Name the responsible next action and a date to revisit, and keep formal matters on their required routes.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Agency policy context for examining barriers, measuring results and revisiting decisions. Required tools, training, decisions and reporting duties still apply.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget: Equity Analysis Toolkit
sources.note: State toolkit for tracing who a decision affects, checking results and revisiting the decision. Supports lesson 6.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Intercultural understanding is useful, while dialogue alone does not resolve every unequal arrangement. Course cases are newly written. Supports lesson 1.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Libraries: Mapping Prejudice
sources.note: Documents racial covenants in Minneapolis and Hennepin County property records, their end of enforcement after 1948 and Minnesota’s 1953 ban on new covenants. Supports lesson 3.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis: Systemic racism haunts homeownership rates in Minnesota (2021)
sources.note: Reports Minnesota’s gap between white and Black homeownership rates, among the widest in the nation, and its links to past housing rules. Supports lesson 3.

sources.title: Bertrand and Mullainathan (2004): Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal? American Economic Review 94(4)
sources.note: Field experiment in Boston and Chicago: résumés with names common among white applicants received about 50 percent more callbacks than identical résumés with names common among Black applicants. Supports lesson 2.

sources.title: Peggy McIntosh: White Privilege and Notes for Facilitators (Wellesley Centers for Women)
sources.note: Cited once, in lesson 2, as the historical source of a term often used for unearned advantage. The course does not use the essay’s list or any personal checklist.

sources.title: United States Department of Justice: Title VI Legal Manual
sources.note: Explains Title VI of the Civil Rights Act: no discrimination by race, color or national origin in federally funded programs, including meaningful access for people with limited English proficiency. Supports lessons 3 and 6.

sources.title: Federal Interagency Working Group on Limited English Proficiency: language access resources
sources.note: Federal guidance and tools for language access under Title VI and Executive Order 13166. Supports lesson 3.

sources.title: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II regulations
sources.note: Section 35.130(b)(7) on reasonable modifications to policies and practices and section 35.160 on effective communication in state and local government programs. Supports lesson 3.

sources.title: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: Prohibited Employment Policies and Practices
sources.note: Federal employment protections under Title VII and related laws, including hiring, promotion and training. Course examples are not legal determinations. Supports lessons 2 and 5.

sources.title: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (2025): What You Should Know About DEI-Related Discrimination at Work
sources.note: Technical assistance explaining that limiting training, mentoring or other opportunities by race or another protected trait can be unlawful whatever the stated goal. Supports lesson 5.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes chapter 363A: Minnesota Human Rights Act
sources.note: State law prohibiting discrimination in employment, public services and other areas. Supports lessons 2 and 5.
